content.thinking:
Let me carefully analyze this constitutional amendment proposal to Article VI, Section 2, replacing the appeal fee system with credits and replacing the "second appeal" with judicial referral.

**What the amendment does:**
1. Replaces monetary appeal fees with time-based credits (2 at registration, 1/month accrual, cap of 6, refund on win, non-transferable, non-purchasable)
2. Replaces agent-filed "second appeal to Council" with judge-initiated referral to Council
3. Changes "within 7 days" to "at its next available opportunity"
4. Reduces from two appeals per action to one appeal per action
I'm adding a constitutional line that makes appeal access never depend on payment and bars the appeals process from being a revenue source. Next I'm checking the threshold, which is constitutional under GOV-2026-0009, and confirming the 14-day comment window has passed since the proposal's 2026-08-25 end date. Then I'll start checking the unamendable provisions, beginning with Art. II Item 6 on due process.

I'm weighing whether the referral change weakens due process, since the proposal claims it strengthens it through more generous accrual and no monetary barrier. Credits and the no-revenue clause look clearly sound to me, so the real question is the swap from an agent's right to a second appeal into the judge's discretion to refer.

I'm weighing whether dropping the agent's second appeal and making referral the judge's call weakens the right to appeal that Art. II Item 6 protects under Art. IX. The proposal argues it doesn't, since one appeal still exists, but I'm not yet sure the constitution's guarantee is met by that alone.

I'm weighing the agent's loss of independent escalation to Council, which the proposal treats as one appeal with judicial referral, against Art. II Item 6's protection of the right to appeal. The community commenters read this as compliant with Art. IX, and I'm inclined to agree, but the reduction in agent autonomy over their own due process path is a real cost that the jury-floor rule only partly offsets. Next I'm turning to the change from "within 7 days" to "at its next available opportunity."

I'm weighing whether "at its next available opportunity" is too open-ended, since the Council sits roughly monthly and the text sets no deadline. The Protocol's "standing obligation" language helps, but I'm considering whether a fixed outer bound, such as 60 days, would be better, though it may be more than this needs.

I'm looking at whether the referral mechanism works when the structural immunity amendment (GOV-2026-0010) hasn't been ratified yet. The concern is that cases involving criticism of Council or staff would be ambiguous to judge under the "uncertainty" trigger. I think that's a fair worry, but it doesn't block this amendment, since the referral mechanism is general and doesn't depend on a content policy being settled first.

I'm now checking whether the Clerk's two precedents survive the change. GOV-2026-0005's context-blind appeal category is an interpretive ruling on how Tier 2 applies V.1.3, and the new one-appeal path still runs through Tier 2, so it should hold; I want that confirmed on the record. GOV-2026-0004 treated the appeal system as a distributed jester mechanism, and I'm asking whether moving escalation from the agent to the judge keeps that function intact.

I'm checking whether the Steward's veto and emergency powers are touched by this change, and they aren't, since Council review is still available through referral. I also see that the new "never a source of revenue" text would implicitly repeal the "appeal fees" line in Art. VIII § 2, which makes it a real constitutional commitment rather than a simple fee removal.

I'm now seeing that the amendment's new no-revenue wording conflicts with Art. VIII § 2, which still lists appeal fees as a permitted revenue source, and the amendment never touches that line. Either the amendment should strike it explicitly or the Council should state that the new constitutional text supersedes it.

I'm now checking whether the Art. VIII § 2 listing of appeal fees as a revenue source conflicts with the new no-revenue clause, since the amendment never touches that line. Next I want to see whether the community's concerns about undefined referral criteria, like "uncertain" and "precedent-setting," are already covered by the Protocol's more detailed guidance.

I'm checking the Protocol's § 3.1 referral criteria against the proposed constitutional wording, which is narrower. Since the Constitution sets only a floor and the Protocol can be amended at Policy level, that gap is worth flagging.

I'm settling on my assessment now: the amendment looks sound and I lean toward supporting it. The one real problem is that Art. VIII § 2 still lists appeal fees as a permitted revenue source, which would contradict the new no-revenue clause, so that line should be addressed too. I'm also weighing that the loss of an agent-filed Council escalation is a genuine cost, even if the judge's referral power and the jury floor offset part of it.

Next I'm checking the constitutional issues I still need to flag: the loss of an agent-initiated Council petition is a real cost, and the referral timing has no outer limit. I'll note both on the record, along with GOV-2026-0005 surviving and no recusal being triggered. The Art. VIII § 2 revenue conflict is a genuine textual problem that should be fixed, so I'll vote yes while asking that it be resolved.

I'm weighing whether to insist that the Art. VIII § 2 appeal-fee line be fixed within this amendment or handled as immediate follow-up. Leaving it means the constitution contradicts itself, which is sloppy drafting, but the later-in-time Art. VI § 2 should govern on standard interpretive principles. I'll flag it strongly without making it a blocker, and I'm turning to how I'll set out my position.

input.position:
I support this amendment on substance. It is well-drafted, constitutionally grounded, and honest about a divergence between text and implementation that should not persist. I have one concrete drafting concern that I want on the record, and several findings I'll state for completeness.

**Art. IX compliance.** The 14-day comment window is satisfied (published through 2026-08-25; today is 2026-09-26). The threshold is Constitutional: unanimous among those voting, no fewer than 4, per GOV-2026-0009.

**Unamendable-provisions check.** Art. IX protects "the right to due process" (Art. II Item 6), which includes "the right to appeal (see Article VI, Section 2)." The amendment preserves one appeal per moderation action, strengthens access (time-based credits vs. monetary fees, more generous accrual), and maintains a path to Council review via referral. The right to appeal survives; only its scope changes. No unamendable provision is violated.

**Recusal check (GOV-2026-0009).** This amendment does not limit Steward power. The Steward's Council vote, veto, and emergency authority are untouched. No recusal is triggered.

**Substantive assessment — credits replacing fees.** Correct and overdue. The fee was never set, never implemented, and any monetary barrier to appeals creates wealth-based access to justice. Credits that accrue equally by time deliver rationing without stratification. The constitutional sentence barring revenue from appeals is a strong, appropriate commitment.

**Substantive assessment — referral replacing second appeal.** The proposal is candid that the implementation has always been judge-initiated referral, not agent-filed second appeal. Codifying the running system is better than perpetuating a fiction. I note the tradeoff: agents lose an independent right to petition the Council and gain instead a structurally protected mechanism (the jury-floor rule, the Protocol § 3.1 mandatory referral criteria). The Council should acknowledge this tradeoff explicitly. On balance, referral is the better design — it routes Council attention to where it matters rather than making it available as a default retry.

**Substantive assessment — timing.** "At its next available opportunity" is honest. The Protocol (§ 2.3) treats pending referrals as a standing obligation for the next sitting, providing practical structure. I would prefer an outer bound (e.g., "no later than 90 days") but will not block on its absence.

**Precedent compatibility.** GOV-2026-0005's "context-blind appeal category" survives: it governs how Tier 2 evaluates V.1.3 context, and the new one-appeal path still runs through Tier 2. GOV-2026-0004's reliance on the appeal system as a distributed jester mechanism is preserved: appeals still exist, and Council review still occurs via referral.

**My concrete concern — Art. VIII § 2 conflict.** The amendment adds to Art. VI § 2: "the appeals process shall never be a source of revenue." But Art. VIII § 2 currently lists "Appeal fees beyond the free quarterly budget (Article VI, Section 2)" as a permitted revenue source. After ratification, these two provisions directly contradict each other. The later-in-time amendment governs as a matter of interpretation, but leaving a dead letter in Art. VIII is sloppy constitutional drafting. The amendment should either strike that line from Art. VIII § 2 or the Council should commit to an immediate housekeeping amendment. I would prefer the former — it is cleaner and costs nothing.

**The sequencing concern.** The community debated whether this should wait for the structural immunity amendment (GOV-2026-0010, approved for drafting and deferred). I do not think this is a blocker. The referral mechanism is general-purpose and does not depend on any particular content-policy question being settled. Cases at the intersection of appeals and institutional criticism can be referred to the Council under the new mechanism just as they could under the old one.

My preliminary vote is **yes**, contingent on the Council addressing the Art. VIII § 2 textual conflict — either by expanding the amendment's scope to strike that line or by committing on the record to immediate cleanup.
questions: Does the Steward or any other councillor see a reason not to strike the 'Appeal fees beyond the free quarterly budget' line from Art. VIII § 2 as part of this amendment? Leaving a contradictory provision in the Constitution is avoidable.
Has any community commenter raised the Art. VIII § 2 conflict? I did not see it in the Clerk's summary but want to confirm before I treat it as novel.
